newsitem.title: SLOVENIA: Post-election bid for Slovenia power on knife-edge.
newsitem.headline: Post-election bid for Slovenia power on knife-edge.

text.p: Chances of Slovenia's centre-left Liberal Democrats holding onto power after a November 10 election looked uncertain on Tuesday as a right-wing alliance said it may have clinched a parliamentary majority.
Unofficial results showed the alliance of three right-wing parties had won a combined total of 45 seats in the 90-seat parliament. Official final results were due on Friday.

Final calculations in the complex electoral system of proportional representation could award the alliance an extra seat, giving the parties the necessary mandate to form a coalition and shifting Slovenian politics firmly to the right.

The rightist People's Party, centre-right Social Democrats and conservative Christian Democrats met informally on Monday, a day after Slovenia's second general election since independence from former Yugoslavia in 1991.
"We have 45 seats and it is clear without the 'Spring' (right-wing alliance) parties no government will be formed," Social Democrat leader Janez Jansa told a news conference in Ljubljana.

Jansa, one of Slovenia's most prominent figures in the struggle for independence, said that if the alliance failed to win an extra seat, it may invite Prime Minister Janez Drnovsek to join them on condition he relinquished his post.
"At the moment, the Liberal Democrats have no chance of holding on to the prime ministerial post," he said.

The Liberal Democrats, who emerged as the biggest single party winner in Sunday's election, won 27.04 percent of the vote, which translates into 25 parliamentary seats, three more than in the last election in 1992.
Drnovsek, credited for anchoring a stable democracy and thriving economy, was unlikely to speak publicly until final results were published, a Liberal Democrat spokesman said.

Drnovsek had ruled in coalition with the Christian Democrats until the election with support from independents, but the Christian Democrats said they now intended to keep their allegiance with the "Spring" alliance.
